newsitem.title: USA: Sallie Mae reorganization plan lacks holder support.
newsitem.headline: Sallie Mae reorganization plan lacks holder support.

text.p: The Student Loan Marketing Association adjourned a special shareholder meeting Thursday until June 5 because it did not receive enough votes for a management-led plan to reorganize into a private company.
The move came after a dissident shareholder group led by current director Albert Lord also failed to gain enough shareholder support last week for an alternative plan.
The dissident group, called the Committee to Restore Value at Sallie Mae, will collect votes on its separate plan until May 29, while the agency will continue tallying on its plan until June 5.
Sallie Mae, a government sponsored enterprise formed by Congress, buys guaranteed loans from lenders so that they have funds to make more loans.

The management wants Sallie Mae to retain its current focus while engaging in other businesses, such as servicing consumer loans, providing back-office processing and computer software services. Under Lord's plan, the agency would be privatised and make student loans directly instead.
"The writing is on the wall. There is something about these plans (that shareholders) do not like," said Lawrence Hough, Sallie Mae's president and chief excecutive told reporters.
"Neither plan enjoys the support of enough votes for a majority and, therefore, we've got some work to do."
Sallie Mae officials said Thursday some 21 million votes so far had been cast in favour of management's plan, while the same amount voted against it.
That leaves about 20 percent of shareholder votes still uncast for management's plan, according to company officials.

"It's clear that the vast majority of our shareholders want privatisation, but many of them have concerns about board control and board representation," Hough said. He said Sallie Mae is open to making changes regarding the board composition.

Both reorganization proposals aim to carry out Congress' mandate when it enacted legislation last year requiring the government-sponsored enterprise, which has nearly $50 billion in assets, to either become a private business or be liquidated altogether.
Despite opposition between management and Lord's group, Hough said Sallie Mae officials want to negotiate over the differences and have already held private meetings this week.
But he indicated the negotiations will centre around the management's plan. "I want to work with a board that is going to support the business plan of this company," Hough said.
Lord told reporters so far the company's "best offer" in these negotiations was to grant the group four seats out of 16, a plan that does not satisfy his group.
Sallie Mae's stock fell 41.25 to $117.125 on the New York Stock Exchange at mid-afternoon.
